design_detail: Narrative review with a reported literature search (PubMed and cross-references, 6 July 2024; 13 publications: 10 experimental studies and 3 surveys) on whether the alcohol hangover is caused by dehydration and whether drinking water prevents or relieves it, from the Utrecht hangover research group. It summarizes old biomarker studies of diuresis, hormones and electrolytes, student surveys of remedy use, and adds the authors' own re-analysis of an earlier naturalistic study (people walking the Samaria Gorge in Crete the day after drinking), correlating the amount of water drunk with hangover severity and thirst in the 176 walkers who had a hangover.
can_establish: As summarized, what small physiological studies found about fluid balance during hangover, how students rate water as a remedy, and, from the authors' re-analysis of their own data, whether the amount of water people drank on a hangover day was associated with how their hangover and thirst changed over that day.
cannot_establish: Whether drinking water prevents or relieves a hangover: no randomized trial existed by the authors' own account, the survey figures are respondents' ratings of how well water worked, and the re-analysis is correlational, with people who felt worse drinking more water.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review). Re-analysed study: 307 people who completed the 15.8-km Samaria Gorge walk and filled in surveys on the bus before and after it (Verster, Anogeianaki et al., 2020, as described) (p. 14). Surveys: 462 and 826 Dutch students (p. 14). Experimental studies: 1 to 19 men in 1942 to 1982, plus 13 men (2018), 90 volunteers (2019) and 214 participants (2020) (pp. 12-15).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Human studies investigating water consumption or dehydration in relation to hangover; reviews, commentaries, animal studies and non-English articles excluded; conference abstracts included because of the paucity of literature (p. 12).
sample.demographics: Walkers with a hangover had drunk a mean of 3.0 (SD 1.8) alcoholic drinks the evening before (p. 14); other demographics not given.
sample.selection_effects: A small, partly unpublished literature (two conference abstracts) dominated by the authors' own group; the walkers were tourists doing a long hike in the heat, with many more ways to lose and drink fluid than on an ordinary hangover day.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported amount of water drunk during the walk (re-analysis); self-reported use of water as a remedy (surveys); measured fluid intake or hormones in the old experiments.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: walkers drank a mean of 2.7 (SD 0.7) litres of water during the walk (p. 14); in the naturalistic hangover study the evening before averaged 12.4 (SD 4.4) drinks (p. 13); the experimental studies gave, for example, 1.5 to 2.3 g of ethanol per kg or six pints of beer (pp. 13-14).

comparison.controls: None in the re-analysis (correlation across walkers); an alcohol-free control day in the naturalistic study; control conditions in some of the old experiments.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Food, sleep, heat, exertion and the amount of alcohol were not accounted for in the correlations; the authors note that most studies did not control for food, physical activity or sleep (p. 15).

outcomes.instruments: Single-item hangover severity and thirst ratings from 0 (absent) to 10 (extreme); survey ratings of remedy efficacy from 0 to 10; urine flow, plasma hormones, electrolytes and acid-base measures in the experiments (pp. 12-15).
outcomes.validity_norms: Single-item ratings; no validated hangover scale in the re-analysis.
outcomes.operationalization: Dehydration indexed by thirst, urine output, hormones and electrolytes; benefit of water indexed by correlations between water drunk and changes in hangover and thirst ratings.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None in the re-analysis (more than a dozen correlations at p < 0.05).

analysis.effect_sizes: Re-analysis (Spearman, n = 176): water drunk against hangover severity before, during and after the walk r = 0.176 (p = 0.019), 0.243 (p < 0.001) and 0.229 (p = 0.002); against change in hangover severity r = 0.103 (p = 0.174), 0.017 (p = 0.828) and 0.066 (p = 0.388); against thirst r = -0.028, -0.001 and 0.059, and against change in thirst r = -0.023, 0.061 and 0.046, all non-significant (pp. 14-15; signs checked on the rendered page). Survey ratings of water as a remedy: 5.8 of 10 for water while hungover; 5.2 (SD 2.4, N = 618) for water during drinking and 5.6 (SD 2.6, N = 502) for water before bed (p. 14).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Narrative review; the re-analysis was not prespecified.
analysis.selective_reporting: The re-analysis restricted to walkers with a hangover is presented as more appropriate than the original full-sample analysis; the choice was made after the original publication.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Signs of dehydration (thirst, hormonal changes) after drinking were mild and short-lived in small old studies, while hangover lasted all day; students rate water as a moderately effective remedy; and among walkers with a hangover, those who drank more water had worse hangovers but the amount drunk was not related to how their hangover or thirst changed during the day.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions (pp. 9, 17) state that water was not effective in relieving the hangover and that water during or directly after drinking is not effective in preventing it, and that hangover and dehydration are independent consequences of drinking caused by different mechanisms. No trial of water was available (the authors say so on p. 16), the survey figures are ratings rather than measured effects, and the correlational re-analysis cannot separate the effect of water from the fact that people who felt worse drank more; the mechanistic statements in the conclusions go beyond the evidence reviewed.

timeline.event: Jayawardena et al., systematic review of interventions for hangover (cited in the Introduction)
Verster, van Rossum and Scholey on the unknown safety and efficacy of hangover treatments (cited in the Introduction)
This review: no trial of water for hangover found; authors' re-analysis of the Samaria Gorge data.
Imai et al.: first randomized crossover trial of water drunk during drinking, 13 men, no detectable effect on next-morning symptoms (not part of this review)

replication.where_it_stands: Whether water prevents or relieves hangover remains untested in adequately sized trials; the one later trial was small and found no detectable effect.

funding.funder: This research received no external funding (p. 17).
funding.declared_conflicts: A.S. has held research grants from many food, supplement and drinks companies, including Red Bull and Nutricia-Danone, has consulted for several, and is Chief Scientific Officer for Arepa Nootropics; J.G. is a part-time employee of Nutricia Research and has received grants from several companies and funders; J.C.V. has consulted for Eisai, KNMP, Med Solutions, Mozand, Red Bull, Sen-Jam Pharmaceutical and Toast! in the past three years; the other author declares none (pp. 17-18).
funding.affiliations_note: Utrecht University, TU Dresden, Danone Global Research and Innovation Center, Monash University and Swinburne University; the senior author leads the research group that produced most of the surveys and naturalistic studies reviewed.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial in people drinking as they normally would, comparing a specified amount of water after drinking or on the hangover morning with no added water, with a validated hangover scale, blinded assessment where possible and adequate power for a modest effect.

domains.note: A reproducible PubMed search with two search strings, cross-references and stated exclusions, but one database, English only, and no duplicate screening described.
No formal appraisal; general limitations (old, small, retrospective, uncontrolled) are named in the Limitations section.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The surveys, the naturalistic study and the re-analysed walking study come from the authors' own group, and the key correlations are a new analysis of their own data.
The conclusion that water is not effective is stated as a finding although no trial existed, and causal mechanisms (oxidative stress, inflammation) are asserted in the conclusions.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against water as a hangover remedy
domains.note: Evidence that water changes hormonal markers is discounted, and the possibility that people with worse hangovers drink more water (which would hide a benefit) is not weighed against the conclusion.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). The search is reported, which is better than most narrative reviews, but the evidence is thin and largely from the authors' group, and the conclusions on water go beyond correlations and survey ratings. Cite it for the absence of trials up to July 2024, the student survey figures, and the re-analysis as a correlational finding; any claim resting only on it stays at draft and says its figures are second-hand or the authors' own re-analysis.

key_findings.finding: Three searches on 6 July 2024 (PubMed with alcohol hangover and dehydration, 12 records, 3 eligible; alcohol hangover and water, 44 records, 2 eligible; then cross-references, 6 articles and 2 abstracts) identified 13 publications, 10 experimental studies and 3 surveys.
key_findings.locator: Literature search; Limitations and future research, 1st paragraph (p. 15)

key_findings.finding: In the authors' re-analysis of 176 walkers with a hangover (mean 3.0, SD 1.8, drinks the evening before; mean 2.7, SD 0.7, litres of water during a 15.8-km walk), more water drunk went with worse hangover before (r = 0.176, p = 0.019), during (r = 0.243, p < 0.001) and after the walk (r = 0.229, p = 0.002), but the amount of water was not related to change in hangover severity (r = 0.103, p = 0.174; r = 0.017, p = 0.828; r = 0.066, p = 0.388).
key_findings.locator: The impact of drinking water on hangover severity, 3rd study (right column, p. 14); continued, 1st paragraph (p. 15)

key_findings.finding: The amount of water drunk during the walk was not correlated with thirst before (r = -0.028), during (r = -0.001) or after (r = 0.059), nor with changes in thirst (r = -0.023, 0.061 and 0.046); hangover severity and thirst correlated before the walk (r = 0.511, p < 0.001) but not during it (r = 0.066).
key_findings.note: Minus signs checked on the rendered page; the text extraction drops them.

key_findings.finding: In the naturalistic study (mean 12.4, SD 4.4, drinks the evening before), hangover severity was higher than on an alcohol-free control day at every hourly rating from 09:30 to 15:30, while thirst was higher only at 09:30 and 10:30.

In a survey of 462 Dutch students, drinking water was the most used hangover remedy (55.8%), followed by sleeping (55.2%), breakfast (52.2%), drinking more alcohol (47.2%), tea (47.0%), coffee (45.5%), paracetamol (45.0%), aspirin (43.1%), vitamins (40.5%) and hangover products (30.7%); water while hungover was rated 5.8 out of 10 for efficacy.
key_findings.locator: The impact of drinking water on hangover severity, 1st study; Fig. 6 (percentages printed as labels; efficacy bars not extracted)

key_findings.finding: In a survey of 826 Dutch students (conference abstract), water during drinking was rated 5.2 (SD 2.4, N = 618) and water before going to bed 5.6 (SD 2.6, N = 502) out of 10 for preventing the next-day hangover; the amount of water was not recorded in either survey.

Old experimental studies found extra urine output mainly in the first two hours of drinking (one person, 1942), hormonal changes in renin, aldosterone and vasopressin during hangover (6 to 10 men), no change in electrolytes during hangover (19 men in 1974; 90 volunteers in 2019) and, in a placebo-controlled trial of 214 people, no change in skin water content.
key_findings.locator: Studies investigating the nexus between alcohol hangover and dehydration (pp. 12-14); right column of p. 15

key_findings.finding: The authors state that no experimental study had specifically tested whether water intake counteracts dehydration or the alcohol hangover.
key_findings.locator: Limitations and future research, end of 2nd paragraph (left column)

reporting_issues.issue: The correlation between hangover severity and thirst after the walk (r = 0.160, p = 0.034) is described as not significant, although p is below 0.05 and no other threshold is stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pattern of hangover-thirst correlations is reported more one-sidedly than the numbers allow.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says there is a rise in blood pH during hangover and, in the same sentence, cites a significant decrease in pH.
reporting_issues.consequence: Internal contradiction; the cited data indicate a decrease (metabolic acidosis).

reporting_issues.issue: The conclusion that electrolyte imbalance plays no role is attributed to Linkola et al. (1978) while describing the study by Ylikahri et al. (1974).
reporting_issues.consequence: Citation error at the top of the left column.

reporting_issues.issue: The legend of Fig. 7 refers to Fig. 6a when crediting the map.
